# Cardinal canon — draft fixes

Exact corrections for the Artometrics / kylesmcauliffe Cardinal draft, checked against GitHub `kylesmcauliffe/cardinal` @ `63a999e` (21 Nov 2026, 11:48 PT) and against Kenneth Whyte, *Hoover: An Extraordinary Life in Extraordinary Times* (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, first edition, 2017).

**Do not edit the draft or the repo in this session.** Each item is for Kyle’s approval. Quotes from the draft are verbatim from `63a999e`. Whyte quotes are verbatim from the 2017 Knopf page-list. Page images are on this log.

Last updated: 2026-11-21 (America/Los_Angeles). §23–25 from Richard White, *Railroaded* (W. W. Norton, 2011), checked against repo @ `0c8c5fb`.

## 1. Swain’s department and the Portland exams
- **Canon:** CANON-001
- **File:** `books/cardinal/ch/3-01-stanford-prototype-hoover.qmd` (also podcast ep04 / draft part-04)
- **Current (l.125):** “Stanford geology professor named Joseph Swain came through Portland recruiting”
- **Corrected:** A professor in Stanford’s inaugural math department, Joseph Swain, administered the Portland entrance exams. Hoover traveled to Portland to take them. Stanford, short of students to fill its dormitories, admitted him on condition that he catch up on geometry.
- **Cite:** Whyte, *Hoover* (Knopf 2017), ch. 2, p. 33. Image: `screenshots/whyte-hoover/p33.png`.

## 2. “Passed mathematics and failed everything else”
- **Canon:** CANON-002
- **Files:** `books/cardinal/ch/3-01-stanford-prototype-hoover.qmd`; `site/corpus/rewrite/chapters/ep4-03-farm-opening-day.md` (“failing every entrance subject except mathematics”); podcast ep05
- **Current:** the “passed mathematics / failed everything else” slogan
- **Corrected:** He struggled and came up short at Portland and was admitted on condition he bone up on geometry. On campus he studied, sat the exams, and failed English. Whyte: “Strictly speaking, he did not earn his degree.”
- **Cite:** Whyte pp. 33, 35. Images: `p33.png`, `p35.png`. Attribute any remaining “failed everything except math” line to its actual source (check Harris) rather than to Whyte.

## 3. “A Nevada mine”
- **Canon:** CANON-003
- **Files:** `books/cardinal/ch/3-01-stanford-prototype-hoover.qmd` l.159; `site/corpus/rewrite/chapters/ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.27; podcast ep05
- **Current (ep5-01 l.27, verbatim):** “His first job after graduating was pushing ore carts in a Nevada mine at two dollars a day.”
- **Corrected:** His first mine job after the last USGS summer with Lindgren was as a mucker at the Reward Mine, then the Mayflower graveyard shift, at Nevada City / Grass Valley, California (Nevada County), at $2 and then $2.50 a day — not in the state of Nevada.
- **Cite:** Whyte, ch. 3, pp. 45–46. Images: `p45.png`, `p46.png`. Do not lean on Whyte’s later flourish at p. 271 (“those same states”) to move the job into the Colorado basin.

## 4. Age when sent to Western Australia
- **Canon:** CANON-005
- **Files:** `ch/3-01` l.164; `ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.27
- **Current (ep5-01 l.27, verbatim):** “In 1897, at twenty-three, he was sent to Western Australia.”
- **Corrected:** In 1897, at twenty-two, he was sent to Western Australia (left San Francisco 24 March 1897; offer dated October 1896). An opener set in August 1897 may still say he was twenty-three (birthday 10 August 1874).
- **Cite:** Whyte pp. 4–5, 49–50, 54.

## 5. “1897–1908. Hoover in Western Australia”
- **Canon:** CANON-004, CANON-016
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/timeline.md` l.54; ledger-snapshot.csv note on 1897-01-01
- **Current (timeline, verbatim):** “1897–1908. Hoover in Western Australia; his Sons of Gwalia mine has air "notably bad." (Whyte ch 5, p. 100)”
- **Corrected:** First tour about eighteen months (arrives May 1897; leaves Australia 11 December 1898). Later returns as London-based operating partner (from mid-January 1902) until the 30 June 1908 exit from Bewick, Moreing. The “notably bad” air finding belongs to the 1905 Royal Commission on the Ventilation and Sanitation of Mines (Whyte, ch. 5, p. 100) — keep the quote, detach it from a ten-year residence.
- **Cite:** Whyte pp. 57, 68, 89, 100, 104. Images: `p57.png`, `p68.png`, `p89.png`, `p100.png`, `p104.png`.

## 6. “Whyte 2021”
- **Canon:** CANON-006

- **Current:** “Whyte 2021, 43”; “Whyte 2021, 100”; “Whyte 2021, 124”
- **Corrected:** Whyte 2017, with the same page numbers (Knopf first edition).
- **Cite:** Copyright page of the 2017 Knopf edition (LCCN 2017015685).

## 7. 1899 role in China
- **Canon:** CANON-011
- **Files:** `ch/3-01` l.190; `ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.57
- **Current (ep5-01 l.57, verbatim):** “In 1899 the firm sent him to China as chief engineer for a mining concern operating at Kaiping, north-east of Tianjin, under a concession from the Chinese government.”
- **Corrected:** In 1899 he went to China as technical adviser to Chang Yen-Mao, who paid his salary of $12,500, to survey gold mines in Chang’s realm. Moreing had a private, likely undisclosed, profit share for him, and Hoover told his brother he would “have charge” of the firm’s Chinese business. Later Chang raised his salary, expanded his role at the Chinese Engineering and Mining Company, and installed him as chief engineer of the newly created Mining Bureau for Chihli — still without yielding control.
- **Cite:** Whyte, ch. 4, pp. 70–71, 76. Images: `p70.png`, `p71.png`, `p76.png`.

## 8. Janin / the clerk story
- **Canon:** CANON-008
- **Files:** `ch/3-01`; `ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.27 (“the recommendation of Louis Janin, a prominent San Francisco mining engineer for whom he clerked”)
- **Current:** the clerkship told as straight fact
- **Corrected:** Janin, educated at Yale and Freiburg, recommended him to Bewick, Moreing. The copyist-to-engineer story is Hoover’s own account, which Whyte calls charming and dubious; Whyte’s documented basis is Hoover’s work on the North Star suit, including a *Mining & Scientific Press* article that matched the defense and did not disclose the Janin tie.
- **Cite:** Whyte pp. 46–48. Images: `p46.png`, `p47.png`.

## 9. Partnership wording (specify, don’t reverse)
- **Canon:** CANON-015
- **Files:** `ch/3-01` ll. 82, 110, 253: “By 1901 he is a partner in the firm” / “By 1901 Hoover was a partner in Bewick, Moreing. By 1908 he was running his own”
- **Current:** true but thin
- **Corrected:** At the end of 1901 he purchased an operating partnership for $40,000, borrowed from the firm, to receive 20 percent of profits over ten years. He sold out as of 30 June 1908 to William Loring for $150,000, under a ten-year restrictive covenant, and opened at 62 London Wall, the same address as Bewick, Moreing. Moreing sued him in 1910 for violating the covenant; settled out of court to Moreing’s advantage.
- **Cite:** Whyte pp. 89, 104, 117. Images: `p89.png`, `p104.png`.

## 10. CRB founding date
- **Canon:** CANON-019
- **File:** `apps/web-of-people/data/ledger-snapshot.csv` event 1914-10-01
- **Current:** dated 1914-10-01, “Hoover organises the Commission for Relief in Belgium; Émile Francqui directs the Belgian Comité National de Secours et d’Alimentation.” The note already admits October 1914 is the month of formal start.
- **Corrected:** Mid-to-late October 1914; Hoover’s informal charter is a letter to Ambassador Page dated 20 October 1914. Add that Francqui, “a former lieutenant for King Leopold II in the Congo,” had overlapped with Hoover for six months in China representing Moreing’s Belgian partners, “They had not gotten along.” Record Whyte’s “Comité Central” alongside the ledger’s “Comité National.”
- **Cite:** Whyte, ch. 7, pp. 142–144. Images: `p142.png`, `p143.png`, `p144.png`.

## 11. Joyce / party-versus-witness / minutes
- **Canon:** CANON-014
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/timeline.md` (Kaiping “CONTESTED” note); `ch/3-01` Kaiping section; ledger 1905-03-01 (judgment already correctly dated)
- **Current:** timeline treats Hoover’s party-vs-witness conflict as contested, “say so in one sentence.”
- **Corrected:** Keep the 17 January–1 March 1905 trial and Joyce’s finding that the 19 February 1901 memorandum was binding and that the breach was “a flagrant breach of faith.” Add: Hoover was not a named defendant (suit filed 7 May 1903). Whyte, weighing Hoover’s earlier letters against the testimony, calls the testimony “disingenuous.” Whyte also writes that Hoover later obtained and apparently destroyed every copy of the court minutes he could find (one set has survived).
- **Cite:** Whyte, ch. 5, pp. 94, 100–102. Images: `p94.png`, `p100.png`, `p101.png`, `p102.png`.

## 12. Trusteeship enrichment (not a reversal)
- **Canon:** CANON-018
- **Files:** ledger 1912-01-01; `ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.82 already quotes “in circumstances as cloudy as the awarding of his geology degree” but cites “Whyte 2021, 124”
- **Current:** year-only trustee date; citation year wrong
- **Corrected:** Autumn 1912. Fix the citation to Whyte 2017, p. 124. Add the residency dodge, Jordan kicked up to chancellor, Branner installed, and — attributed to Whyte — that Hoover wanted the presidency himself.
- **Cite:** Whyte, ch. 6, p. 124. Image: `p124.png`.

## Optional enrichments (no contradiction)
- Marriage and sailing: 10 and 11 February 1899, SS *Coptic* (Whyte pp. 69, 71). `ep5-01` l.35 already says they sailed the next day.
- Moreing’s 1898 loan: £200,000 / US$1 million at 12 percent, no equity; gold-mine survey as the opening (pp. 70–71).
- Kaiping share watering: 625,000 shares to Moreing and “mostly Belgian associates” for no cash; £500,000 debenture at 6 percent (pp. 85–86). Hoover’s own estimate of “some $50 million worth of high-grade coal” (pp. 100–101).
- Colorado River Compact, Hoover at Commerce, Boulder Canyon, 50-50 basins, “freed from a generation of litigation…” (pp. 270–271). New ledger-candidate. Do not cite Whyte for the 1930 Wilbur naming or Six Companies.
- *De Re Metallica*, 1912, 289 woodcuts, AHR “noteworthy monument…” (pp. 119–120).
- Lou Henry Hoover House: San Juan Hill, 57 rooms, 12,500 sq ft, $170,000 (p. 240). Do not take the 1920 year or “later the president’s house” from Whyte.
- Foreign Office on Kaiping: “Yankee man of straw acting for Moreing,” “fleeced,” “a case of rogues falling out” (p. 93).
- *Principles of Mining* (1909) from Stanford and Columbia lectures; Jordan’s letter to Taft (pp. 117, 122).

## Do not “fix” from Whyte alone
- 1919 War Collection telegram, $50,000 pledge, and Belgian Congo / Ruanda-Urundi documents (ledger 1919-01-01, 1919-04-22, 1919-06-01): Whyte is silent. Leave on existing sources (CANON-023).
- 17 September 1930 Wilbur naming and 1 February 1931 Six Companies: Whyte is silent. Leave on Stevens / McCartney / Denton (CANON-020).
- Wilbur “remaining Stanford’s president” while Interior Secretary: not in the Whyte cabinet-making passage (p. 364).
- Opening-day 555 vs. 559: Whyte supports 559; do not silently drop 555 until its source is produced (CANON-007).
- Harris’s typhoid / Branner medical bills vs. Whyte’s measles-only notice (Run 1): still needs a second source.

## 23. Contract and Finance Company and Chinese headcount: “twice,” “disappeared,” 10–12 thousand
- **Canon:** CANON-053, CANON-065
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/research/chronology.md` l.42; `site/corpus/rewrite/research/concordance.md` l.33, l.41; `books/cardinal/ch/2-09-railroads-first-monopoly.qmd` l.211
- **Current:** chronology l.42: “Charles Crocker recruits over 15,000 Chinese laborers … bills the federal government triple the actual construction costs.” concordance l.33: “writing contracts to themselves at triple market rates, keeping no accounting ledgers, and burning the books when subpoenaed by the Pacific Railway Commission.” concordance l.41: “the 15,000 Chinese railroad workers.” ch/2-09 l.211: “the accounts of the Contract and Finance Company were destroyed before a congressional investigation could examine them.”
- **Corrected:** Use “roughly twice the actual cost of construction per mile,” the PRC estimate in White ch. 1 ¶80, and “when threatened with a congressional investigation, the books disappeared, never to resurface” (ch. 1 ¶94). Do not say “triple” or “burned when subpoenaed by the PRC.” The PRC was created in 1887; the books had already vanished. For ch/2-09 l.211, change “were destroyed” to “disappeared.” For Chinese headcount, use “roughly eleven thousand at peak periods” (White ch. 7 ¶49, Strobridge PRC testimony), with Chew’s 5,190 peak-month figure as the low bound. Draft ch/2-09 l.129 (“between ten and twelve thousand”) is fine. Replace “15,000” unless Chang supports it (check when Chang is read).

## 24. Stanford estate suit: amount, timing, chapter
- **Canon:** CANON-060
- **Files:** `books/cardinal/appendix-b-ledger.qmd` l.84; `books/cardinal/ch/2-13-widow-will-machine.qmd` l.92; `site/corpus/rewrite/research/chronology.md` l.77–79; `concordance.md` l.35
- **Current:** ledger l.84: “Estate frozen; the federal government sues for $15 million. The university nearly closes.” chronology l.77: “The federal government files suit to seize the Stanford estate to recoup the $15 million …”; l.79 sources “Richard White, *Railroaded*, Ch. 11.”
- **Corrected:** The claim was **$15,237,000** (United States v. Stanford, 161 U.S. 412, 1896; dismissed, affirmed March 2, 1896, because the Pacific Railroad Acts imposed no personal stockholder liability). White has Olney preparing the suit “unwillingly and under pressure,” relying on California stockholder liability. White’s account is in **ch. 9 ¶103–108**, not ch. 11. “$15 million” is an acceptable rounding. Say the suit came within months of the death, not at it. Add the outcome. Chronology l.78, “financing faculty salaries out of her personal jewelry allowance,” is not in White *Railroaded*. Source it elsewhere (White, *Who Killed Jane Stanford?*, when read) or cut it.

## 29. The 1867 strike date and season (Ep. 2)
- **Canon:** CANON-083
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/chapters/ep2-06-the-summit.md` l.17 (“In late May … the Chinese went on strike,” via Ambrose) and l.99 (ledger “25 June 1867”); `site/corpus/rewrite/timeline.md` l.28 (“1867, late May”) and l.30 (ledger Jun 25); `appendix-b-ledger.qmd` (Jun 25).
- **Fix:** the strike began **Monday, June 24, 1867**. E. B. Crocker’s June 27 letter to Huntington says “last Monday,” and June 24, 1867 was a Monday (Chang p. 151; NPS). It lasted about eight days. Replace “late May.” Correct the ledger from Jun 25 to Jun 24, or say “June 24–25” with a note. Keep the E. B. Crocker “hardest blow” quote, but date it to his June 28, 1867 letter. Chang’s wording: “this strike of the chinamen is the hardest blow we have had here.”

## 30. Strike details stated too flatly (Ep. 2)
- **Canon:** CANON-083
- **Files:** `ep2-02-the-store.md` l.204–210, `ep2-04-the-surveyor.md` l.261–267 and `books/cardinal/ch/2-09-railroads-first-monopoly.qmd` l.234–240 and l.77–78 (an identical paragraph: “an end to the practice of whipping … Crocker broke it … by cutting off the food supply”); `ep2-07-ten-miles.md` l.13, 15, 67 (“starved back to work”); `research/concordance.md` l.45 and `research/blueprint.md` l.87 (“in the high desert,” “cutting off supply trains,” “starved into submission”).
- **Fix:**
  - (a) The whipping/free-movement demand comes from one paper, the *Sacramento Union*; Chang and the Stanford project note that no other source repeats it. Write “one newspaper reported they also protested….”
  - (b) Supplies were cut off: Charles Crocker later claimed he did it; E. B. Crocker wrote at the time that the Chinese agents stopped provisions. “Crocker cut off provisions, by his own later account” is safe.
  - (c) The strike was in the Sierra, Cisco to Truckee, not the “high desert.” Nothing in Chang supports “supply trains.”
  - (d) Optional nuance: wages for experienced men rose above $35 after the strike (Chang p. 157), so “starved into submission” overstates the outcome.
- **Also:** ep2-02 and ep2-04 carry the same strike paragraph verbatim, apparently a duplication. Flag for the editor.

## 31. Stanford’s pre-strike warning: wrong recipient, wrong title (Ep. 2)
- **Canon:** CANON-084
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/timeline.md` l.29 (“Stanford himself relayed the warning … to Huntington”); `ep2-06-the-summit.md` l.31 (“to Huntington”; “If the governor in Sacramento knew…”).
- **Fix:** Stanford wrote to **Mark Hopkins**, May 18, 1867 (Huntington Letters; Chang p. 150 n.). He reported unhappiness among Chinese contracted under “Sisson.” He was CPRR president; his governorship ended in Dec. 1863. Write “the railroad’s president, the former governor.” Better still, use the Sisson link: Clark W. Crocker was a Sisson partner (CANON-082).

## 32. Chronology entry: numbers and sources (research files)
- **Canon:** CANON-065, CANON-082, CANON-083
- **Files:** `site/corpus/rewrite/research/chronology.md` l.41–45 (“recruits over 15,000 Chinese laborers”; Contract and Finance Company “bills the federal government triple”; sourced to “Chang ch. 3–7; White ch. 3”); `research/concordance.md` l.41 (“15,000 Chinese railroad workers”).
- **Fix:**
  - Peak numbers: Crocker gave about 10,000 (fall 1868, Chang p. 195), and White gives about 11,000 (CANON-065). The company *sought* 15,000 to 20,000 (Stanford’s reports, Chang pp. 124, 139). Use “10,000–12,000 at peak” as the chapters already do.
  - Chang does not discuss the Contract and Finance Company or “triple” billing. Drop Chang as a source for that sentence and source it to White, if White supports the figure (unchecked here).

## 33. CANON-075 and CANON-078 closed (web checks)
- **CANON-075 (Frisbie):** the AG Report 1861 p. 131 has Frisbie promoted brigadier general on Nov. 14, 1861, under Gov. Downey, before Stanford’s Jan. 10, 1862 inauguration. Brechin’s “appointed by Governor Stanford” is unsupported. `podcast/ep01-the-ledger.md` l.196 needs no change. If anyone expands it, write “a militia general from 1861.”
- **CANON-078 (UC–Los Alamos):** an OSRD letter of intent took effect Jan. 1, 1943; contract W-7405-ENG-36 with the Manhattan Engineer District was signed Apr. 20, 1943, retroactive to Jan. 1 (Manhattan District History, Project Y, LAMS-2532 §1.11; LANL). `books/cardinal/ch/3-09-total-war-filter.qmd` l.201 and `ep5-06-radio-lab.md` l.45 and 95: check any dates against this.

## Do not import from Chang
- “More than 175 million square miles of public land” (p. 63–64). That is impossible: the whole US is about 3.8M sq mi. Don’t use it; cite White or a federal land-grant source for acreage.
- Stanford “assuming office in 1861” (p. 66). He was inaugurated Jan. 10, 1862 (CANON-081).
- “Congress overrode his veto” of the 1882 Exclusion bill (p. 232). Wrong: Arthur’s Apr. 4, 1882 veto stood, and he signed the revised 10-year Act on May 6, 1882 (Senate sustained the veto 29–21 on Apr. 5; senate.gov veto list; National Archives).
- “Congress on April 9, 1869, determined the two lines would meet” (p. 200). The joint resolution was approved Apr. 10, 1869; Apr. 9 is the Huntington–Dodge agreement.
- Susanville “in western Nevada” (p. 237). It is in Lassen County, California.
- “1,200” deaths as a fact (pp. 227–228). Chang himself concludes “well into the hundreds, if not substantially higher” (CANON-088).
- “The company appealed to the federal government to send ‘5,000 negroes’” (p. 151). The note cites only private letters; no federal request document is identified. Hedge it, or say “the company sought 5,000 freedmen.”
- Stanford “rued his earlier prejudice” (p. 63). This comes from Chang’s own essay and the Cain thesis, with no primary quote in the text. Don’t present it as Stanford’s words.
- The CPRR “began” at Colfax (p. 64). It began at Sacramento (ground broken Jan. 8, 1863).

## Optional enrichments from Chang (no contradiction)
- The Crocker-family commissary loop (CANON-082): the strongest money item. Payroll cash went to the Crocker-partnered contractor, which kept the supply charges.
- “We want 100,000 chinamen here so as to bring the price of labor down” / Huntington’s “half a million” / “a surplus will keep wages low. It is our only remedy for strikes” (CANON-085).
- Crocker under oath: “I think I did” make more money with Chinese labor (CANON-086).
- The PRC provenance of the “buried till spring” quotes: letters to Stanford in 1887 (CANON-089).
- Stanford alone at Promontory; the spike sits in Stanford’s museum (CANON-091).
- Crocker’s “wholesale” pay scheme kept workers nameless: “no list of names was kept” (Chang p. 195).
- Stanford’s 1862 inaugural also attacks big land claimants who “dispossess others from a hundred leagues” (CANON-081). An irony for the land thread.
- The Santa Cruz Mountains tunnel explosion (Nov. 18, 1879; 24–32 Chinese killed) on James G. Fair’s South Pacific Coast line (Chang pp. 234–235). A Peninsula-region beat.

## Lead-chase additions (November 21, 2026)

These notes record later primary/official source checks. They do **not** rewrite earlier sections of this file. New canon rows are CANON-094 through CANON-107, appended after CANON-093 (Chang rows).

### 1883 Stoneman withdrawal (CANON-094)
- **Prior:** Brechin p. 283; CANON-069.
- **Added:** Official UC centennial history cites *San Francisco Evening Bulletin*, February 24, 1883, p. 4, and “Regents Muddle Settled,” *Bulletin*, February 27, 1883, p. 1. Those pages were not independently OCR’d this session (CDNC blocked). The *San Francisco Call*, September 17, 1899, p. 27, is a later narrative. Do not treat spite as the founding motive.

### “Peanut vendor” line (CANON-095)
- **Prior:** Quoted on Brechin p. 283 as “his lawyer.”
- **Corrected attribution:** Alfred A. Cohen, 1876, in *Central Pacific Railroad Company v. Cohen*, printed pamphlet (HathiTrust 012476392). Cohen was a former railroad counsel turned defendant. PDF not in hand this session.

### “Kindergarten” (CANON-096)
- **Corrected:** Not found as an 1883 Stoneman-fight rumor. *Harvard Crimson*, March 25, 1891, attributes “start… with the kindergarten” to Senator Stanford himself. *The First Year at Stanford* (1905) records the newspaper rumor.

### Founding Grant and *Sharon v. Hill* (CANON-097, CANON-098)
- **Added from the primary Grant:** the full November 11, 1885 trustee list, including Irving M. Scott and William M. Stewart as well as Sawyer, Deady, and Field. Source: Stanford 1987 printing of the Grant.
- **Added from 26 F. 337 (December 26, 1885):** Deady wrote; Sawyer sat; Stewart was Sharon’s counsel. Field was not on this panel. Deady’s diary and 1885–86 press criticism remain unread.

### Missionaries quote (CANON-099; was CANON-070)
- **Corrected:** Leland Stanford to David Starr Jordan, August 24, 1892, SC 33a, Box 2, Folder 4. Use the fuller wording, dated. Not a cornerstone address.

### Ross / AEA report (CANON-100)
- **Added:** 1901 *Report of the Committee of Economists* (Internet Archive `reportofcommitte02comm`) pins the May–November 1900 chronology and the committee’s findings. Jane Stanford’s 1900 letters are located in the JLS papers.

### Frisbie (CANON-101; update to CANON-075)
- **Added:** WPA / California Military Museum history cites *Adjutant General Report 1861*, p. 131, for a November 14, 1861, brigadier promotion — before Stanford’s January 10, 1862, inauguration. Do not say Governor Stanford appointed him until that AG page is opened and says so.

### 1919 telegram (CANON-102; update to CANON-023)
- **Added:** Hoover Institution, “Making Hoover History With A Telegram,” publishes the April 22, 1919, text and the Adams clarification. Congo / Ruanda-Urundi documents remain unverified.

### SRI / Swain (CANON-103)
- **Reconfirmed from SRI’s history:** Swain 1925, Hoover as early supporter, incorporation November 6, 1946. “Conceived by President Hoover” remains an overstatement. Gibson p. 156 still unseen.

### Brechin misattributed scenes (CANON-104)
- **Confirmed by full-text search:** Portolá, Stock Farm, Muybridge, “Romanesque-Moorish fortress,” eucalyptus-grove isolation, and a 1906 “purge of dissidents” are not in Brechin. Only p. 283 (and n1 on the Arch) is his Stanford-campus material.

### Pacific Railway Commission case (CANON-105)
- **Confirmed:** *In re Pacific Railway Commission*, 32 F. 241 (C.C.N.D. Cal. August 29, 1887), is the case White cites. Dollar figures remain on White’s PRC table citations.

### Los Alamos contract / Grove nights (CANON-106; update to CANON-078)
- **Added:** April 20, 1943, for the UC operating contract (institutional histories). Grove meeting possibly September 13–14, 1942, not 15–16; hedge until a primary is in hand.

### Walker Blaine / *Oregon* (CANON-107)
- **Split:** UIW’s *Oregon* contract is corroborated; the Walker Blaine introduction remains Hammond-only.

### Still open after this chase
- 1883 *Bulletin* page images; Cohen 1876 pamphlet PDF; Deady diary; Veblen 1909 letters; Pauley/Nichols/McLaughlin archives; McCartney pp. 32–33 and McCone as SRI director (CANON-031); Gibson p. 156; 1919 Congo documents; Cutler as Hoover schoolmate; Consolidated steel replacement figure (CANON-029); Jordan’s $500 Federal Telegraph investment in a ledger.
